Snapline 2.20.0

The Record Screen and Scrolling Capture overlay gets out of your way: the command bar follows what you select, the screen stays bright until you have picked something, and the cursor finally shows what it has been trying to say. The Editor reaches the capture's text, and the Quick Access card's menu and picker are tidied.

Record Screen and Scrolling Capture

  • The command bar follows the selection. Drag a region, pick a window or a display, and the bar moves to sit just below it, centered. When there is no room beneath it flips above; when there is no room either way — a near-full-height region, a maximized window, Full Screen — it tucks inside along the bottom edge. It never covers the Dock or the menu bar, and it stays centered under the selection even as the microphone and camera controls come and go. With nothing selected it rests bottom-center, as before — now truly centered, even with the Dock on one side.
  • The screen dims when you have chosen something, not before. Setting up in the bar — mode, microphone, camera, overlays — happens over the live screen; the dim arrives with the selection, to frame it.
  • The cursor tells the truth. The crosshair, the open hand over a selected region, the closed hand while you move it and the resize arrows on its handles now actually appear on screen, and the open hand shows the instant a drag settles.
  • Settings opens on top. "Customize…" from the camera style menu used to open Settings underneath the overlay, unclickable. The overlay now stands down while Settings is up and comes back when it closes.

Editor

  • View Text and Copy Text join the footer, beside Copy and Save — the same two actions the card, History and the menu bar offer, addressed to the capture you are editing. The text is the capture's: an unsaved crop still copies the whole shot's words.

Quick Access card and History

  • One right-click menu. The card and the History tile share the same grouped menu and the same words: "Pin", "Copy Image" for a still and "Copy File" for a recording or GIF, and Star / Unstar on every kind of capture. History's menu gains the same icons.
  • The Convert picker reads in dark mode. The current format's name no longer disappears into its highlight.
  • The card's frame is keyboard-navigable, and "Use Keyboard on Latest Capture" in the status menu hands it the keyboard on purpose — the card never takes it on its own. Its toggles read as checkboxes to VoiceOver, and the on-state honours Increase Contrast.
  • The picture inside the hover frame wears a light frost so it reads as part of the card rather than a hole in it; the busy spinner stays while the pointer is away; "already compact" names the file's format.

Fixed

  • Exports are the capture's size again. Redact from the card, and Done in Annotate, rendered at the screen's Retina scale — an 808×600 capture came out 1616×1200, four times the pixels and no new detail. Every export now renders one pixel per point.
  • HEIC and WebP captures put their PNG rendition on the clipboard as a promise fulfilled at paste time, so copying is instant; the Redact toggle decodes off the main thread.

Snapline 2.19.0

The Quick Access card that appears after a capture now does the things that used to mean a round trip through the editor: change the format, shrink the file, redact — each in place, each one click.

Quick Access card

  • A new frame around the card. Every action is a labelled cell around the picture — pin, dismiss, convert, copy, edit, redact, view text, copy text, save — and the caption reads the capture's dimensions, size and format. History tiles wear the same frame on hover, so what you learn on the card works in History too.
  • Convert. A PNG, JPEG, HEIC and WebP row switches the capture's format in place: the file in your screenshot folder is replaced, the History entry stays exactly where it was, the old file goes to the Trash, and the new one lands on your clipboard. A format the capture can't be held in is refused before anything is written.
  • Compress. One click cuts a capture's size and reports what it saved: a lossy file is re-encoded at a compact quality, a Retina PNG is redrawn at 1×, and any other PNG becomes an 8-bit palette PNG. A capture that is already compact says so rather than being squeezed twice.
  • Redact. Runs Smart Redact on the shot you just took and bakes the boxes in; press it again and the original comes back. Any capture currently carrying redactions wears a small badge on the card and in History.
  • Choose which actions you see. Settings → Quick Access → Card actions turns Convert, Compress and Redact off individually; an action that is off is gone from the card and its menu, not greyed out.
  • Clearer glyphs. Copy Text and View Text no longer look like twins: Copy Text takes the Live Text viewfinder, View Text a text window under a glass — on the card, in History and in the menu bar.

Export

  • HEIC and WebP join the export formats. Settings → General offers all four, with one Quality slider covering every lossy format. Both are far smaller than PNG and both keep transparency, and both go on the clipboard with a PNG alongside so they paste into apps that can't read them.
  • Save panels offer the file's own type instead of always proposing PNG.

Snapline 2.18.0

  • Runs on macOS 14 Sonoma. The minimum system version is now macOS 14, where it was macOS 15. Everything works on 14 except Translation in the Text View, which needs macOS 15; on 14 the Text View simply shows no translation bar.
  • Pixelate is the new default redaction style. New redactions in the editor and from Smart Redact are pixelated unless you have chosen a style. Solid is still one click away, and it remains the only style image analysis can't undo, so pick it for anything sensitive.
  • QR and barcode detection is more robust. When Vision's default detector finds nothing in a capture, Snapline retries with the classic detector, so codes are still found on Macs where the newer detector comes up empty.
  • The recording bar now sits above the Dock instead of overlapping its icons.

Show your clicks and keys in screen recordings

  • Highlight Clicks: every mouse click draws a brief expanding ring at the pointer — dual-tone, so it reads against any background. Display and region recordings.
  • Show Keystrokes: the keys you press appear in a capsule at the bottom of the movie, with shortcuts in the same ⌃⌥⇧⌘ symbols as the Shortcuts pane. Needs the Input Monitoring permission, asked once at the toggle; a recording never fails over it — refused access just means no capsule, and Snapline says so.
  • Both overlays are drawn into the recorded frames, so trims, GIF conversions, and shares keep them. The toggles live in the Record Screen bar and Settings → Recording, are remembered, and ship off. Worth knowing: Show Keystrokes records what you type — ordinary text included — into the video.

Snapline 2.16.0

Capture with Self-Timer: frame the region first, watch the countdown, and the shot fires by itself.

Capture

  • Capture with Self-Timer. Frame the region first, then a visible countdown runs — and the shot fires by itself. The delay is for staging: open the menu or tooltip you want inside the frame while the timer counts. Selection works exactly like a normal region capture (releasing the drag starts the timer — no extra confirm), and the countdown sits inside the region with the seconds, an Esc hint, and a ✕ to cancel. Nothing steals focus, so the menu you stage stays open, and the countdown never appears in the shot.
  • Pick 3, 5, or 10 seconds from the new status-menu item beside the Self-Timer setting — its top row remembers your last-used delay for a one-click repeat — or bind a shortcut in Settings → Shortcuts (it ships unbound). A canceled timer saves nothing and says so.
  • The invisible delay is gone. If you keep a sticky Self-Timer default set, region and main-display captures now show this same live countdown instead of silently stalling before the crosshair — same delay, visible and cancellable.

Snapline 2.15.0

History learns starred captures. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit.

History

  • History learns starred captures. Star anything worth keeping and it survives the retention sweep unconditionally — it never expires, and a starred card asks before a manual delete goes through. Star from the card's hover control or its Star/Unstar menu item; a starred capture wears a badge at rest. The History toolbar gains a Starred filter that combines with search.

Robustness

  • Fixed: Snapline could quit itself and not come back after you answered the Screen Recording prompt. The relaunch waited a fixed half-second before reopening, which could fire while the old copy was still shutting down — so nothing came back, and no crash report explained it. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit, and when it can't reopen safely it stays running and tells you instead of vanishing. The prompt for one permission no longer triggers a relaunch offer for another.
  • Also fixed: the camera bubble no longer scans for cameras on the main thread, which could stall the Record Screen bar (and probe for nearby iPhones) each time it opened; its window now closes cleanly instead of racing an in-flight animation; and the bubble's style controls no longer risk a crash from a settings change or a removed gradient stop.
